chapter.name: Atmosphere and Climate
chapter.blurb: Composition and layers of the atmosphere, weather and climate elements, India's seasons, the monsoon, and climate change with the Punjab floods case study.

scope_in.item: Composition of the atmosphere and its importance
Five layers of the atmosphere and their features
Weather and climate; temperature, humidity, precipitation, air pressure, wind, land and sea breezes
Four IMD seasons of India and the traditional six seasons
South-west and north-east monsoons, importance and historical knowledge of the monsoon
Climate change, greenhouse gases, carbon footprint and the Punjab floods 2025 case study

concepts.name: Composition of the atmosphere
concepts.description: The atmosphere as a blanket of gases held by gravity, its main gases, water vapour and dust and why the atmosphere matters.
concepts.idea: The atmosphere is a mixture of gases that protects life, controls temperature and produces weather.
concepts.rule: Nitrogen and oxygen are the two most abundant gases. Others include carbon dioxide (0.04%), argon (0.93%), helium, neon, ozone. Water vapour is generally 0.1 to 0.4 per cent and helps form clouds and rain. The atmosphere shields us from ultraviolet radiation and traps heat.
concepts.example: The atmosphere is pulled around the Earth by gravity; density is highest near the surface.

questions.q: The atmosphere is
questions.a: a blanket of air around the Earth held by gravity
o: a blanket of air around the Earth held by gravity
a layer of water that covers the Earth and is held by gravity
a layer of rock that covers the Earth and is held by gravity
a layer of ice that covers the poles and is held by gravity

questions.q: The two most abundant gases in the atmosphere are
questions.a: nitrogen and oxygen

questions.q: The atmosphere is held around the Earth by ____.
questions.a: gravity

questions.q: Water vapour in the atmosphere generally ranges from
questions.a: 0.1 to 0.4 per cent

questions.q: The atmosphere protects us by
questions.a: shielding us from harmful radiation such as ultraviolet radiation
o: shielding us from harmful radiation such as ultraviolet radiation
making the Earth colder always, so that life is safe
blocking all sunlight that reaches the Earth's surface
creating earthquakes that release the Earth's heat

questions.q: The atmosphere regulates the Earth's temperature by
questions.a: trapping some of the Sun's energy and preventing it from escaping into space
o: trapping some of the Sun's energy and preventing it from escaping into space
blocking all heat so that none of it reaches the ground
sending heat to the core so that the surface stays cool
cooling the oceans only and leaving the land unchanged

questions.q: Water vapour is important because it
questions.a: plays a role in cloud formation and precipitation
o: plays a role in cloud formation and precipitation
makes the air heavy so that it sinks to the ground
creates wind directly by moving from place to place
forms the ozone layer high above the ground

questions.q: The composition of the atmosphere
questions.a: also varies with altitude
o: is the same at every height

questions.q: Why is the atmosphere vital for living beings?
questions.a: It is a mixture of gases needed for life, it shields us from harmful radiation, it regulates temperature by trapping the Sun's energy and it produces weather.
s: Gases needed for life or shielding from radiation

questions.q: Which gas makes up 0.04 per cent of the atmosphere?
questions.a: carbon dioxide

questions.q: Argon makes up about 0.93 per ____ of the atmosphere.
questions.a: cent

questions.q: Besides gases, the atmosphere also contains
questions.a: water vapour and tiny dust particles
o: water vapour and tiny dust particles
sand dunes blown in from the deserts of the Earth
glaciers that float in the air above the poles
volcanoes that throw out gases and rocks

questions.q: Name four gases found in the atmosphere, mentioning the two most abundant.
questions.a: Nitrogen and oxygen (the most abundant), carbon dioxide, argon (also helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone, hydrogen).
s: Nitrogen and oxygen as the most abundant

questions.q: Where is the density of air highest and how does it change upwards?
questions.a: Air is densest near the Earth's surface and its density decreases with altitude.

questions.q: Explain the importance of water vapour in the atmosphere.
questions.a: Its amount varies, generally 0.1 to 0.4 per cent. It plays a significant role in cloud formation and precipitation, and so in weather. Warm air can hold more of it.
s: States the amount or that it varies
Link to weather or warm air holding more

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Nitrogen and oxygen are essential to life and are the most abundant gases
o: Nitrogen and oxygen are essential to life and are the most abundant gases
Carbon dioxide is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere
Argon is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere
Dust is the most abundant component of the atmosphere

questions.q: The chapter asks: what would happen if there were no atmosphere? Give two consequences using the chapter.
questions.a: There would be no shield from ultraviolet radiation, no gases to breathe, no trapping of heat to regulate temperature and no clouds, rain or weather.

questions.q: Explain how the atmosphere influences weather and climate.
questions.a: It contains water vapour that forms clouds and precipitation, it holds heat and regulates temperature, and it exerts pressure and creates winds. Together these determine temperature, humidity and air pressure, the key elements of weather and climate.

questions.q: Ravi says the atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Nitrogen and oxygen are the most abundant gases. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04 per cent.
s: Names nitrogen and oxygen or the 0.04 per cent value

questions.q: Make a simple pie-chart plan showing the atmosphere's gases and name the labels you would use.
questions.a: Label nitrogen and oxygen as the two largest parts, then argon (0.93%), carbon dioxide (0.04%) and small parts for other gases and water vapour.
s: Nitrogen and oxygen as the largest sectors
Water vapour or other gases added

concepts.name: Layers of the atmosphere
concepts.description: The five layers of the atmosphere, their heights, temperature behaviour and features.
concepts.idea: The atmosphere is divided into layers by changes of temperature and density with height.
concepts.rule: Troposphere (about 12 km): weather, temperature falls with height. Stratosphere (up to 50 km): ozone layer, clear for aeroplanes. Mesosphere (up to 80 km): temperature falls, meteors burn. Thermosphere (80-700 km): temperature rises rapidly, radio waves reflected, auroras. Exosphere: uppermost, very thin.
concepts.example: Nearly all weather phenomena such as rain, fog and hail occur in the troposphere.

questions.q: The lowest and most important layer of the atmosphere is the
questions.a: troposphere

questions.q: The ozone layer is found in the
questions.a: stratosphere

questions.q: The uppermost layer of the atmosphere is the ____.
questions.a: exosphere

questions.q: The average height of the troposphere is about
questions.a: 12 km

questions.q: In the troposphere the temperature
questions.a: decreases with increasing altitude
o: increases with altitude, as one goes up from the ground
stays constant at every height above the ground
is always zero, however high one goes

questions.q: Nearly all weather phenomena occur in the
questions.a: troposphere

questions.q: Most meteorites entering from space burn up in the
questions.a: mesosphere

questions.q: The thermosphere helps radio transmission because it
questions.a: reflects radio waves back towards the Earth
o: reflects radio waves back towards the Earth
absorbs all radio waves so that none reach the ground
blocks the Sun so that the ground stays cool
makes clouds that carry radio waves to the ground

questions.q: Why is the stratosphere ideal for flying aeroplanes?
questions.a: It is free of clouds and other weather disturbances, so flying is smooth and safe.

questions.q: The stratosphere extends up to about
questions.a: 50 km

questions.q: The thermosphere extends from 80 to ____ km.
In which layer does temperature rise very rapidly with altitude?
questions.a: thermosphere

questions.q: Name the five layers of the atmosphere in order from the ground upwards.
questions.a: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere.

questions.q: What are auroras and where do they occur?
questions.a: They are colourful displays of light seen near the poles. Charged particles of the solar wind are directed to the magnetic poles and make atmospheric gases glow. They occur in the thermosphere.
s: Colourful light near the poles caused by solar wind

questions.q: Describe the troposphere.
questions.a: It is the most important layer, about 12 km high on average. Temperature decreases with altitude. The air we breathe, most of the water vapour and clouds are here, and nearly all weather such as rain, fog and hail occurs here.

questions.q: Temperature decreases with altitude only in
questions.a: the troposphere (and the mesosphere)
o: the thermosphere, where temperature rises with height
the stratosphere only, where the ozone layer lies
the exosphere, where the atmosphere merges into space

questions.q: Why does the ozone layer in the stratosphere matter?
questions.a: It filters the Sun's harmful radiation, including ultraviolet radiation, and so protects living beings.

questions.q: Distinguish between the troposphere and the stratosphere.
questions.a: Troposphere: about 12 km high, temperature decreases with height, contains air we breathe, water vapour, clouds and all weather. Stratosphere: extends to 50 km, free of clouds and weather, contains the ozone layer and is used by aeroplanes.

questions.q: Meera says weather like rain occurs in the exosphere. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Nearly all weather phenomena occur in the troposphere. The exosphere is the uppermost layer with very thin air.

questions.q: Draw a labelled sketch plan of the layers of the atmosphere with heights.
questions.a: Draw horizontal layers up the page and label: troposphere (about 12 km), stratosphere (to 50 km, ozone), mesosphere (to 80 km), thermosphere (80-700 km) and exosphere at the top.
s: One feature for each of at least two layers

concepts.name: Weather, climate and their elements
concepts.description: The difference between weather and climate and the elements of temperature, humidity, precipitation, air pressure and wind, including land and sea breezes.
concepts.idea: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere; climate is the long-term average.
concepts.rule: Weather: hour-to-hour and day-to-day conditions. Climate: sum of weather conditions over a large area, usually thirty years or more. Elements: temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind, air pressure. Wind flows from high to low pressure.
concepts.example: Sea breeze blows from sea to land in the day, land breeze from land to sea at night.

questions.q: Weather refers to
questions.a: the hour-to-hour and day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere
o: the hour-to-hour and day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere
the average conditions over thirty years at a place
the seasons of the year and the months in each of them
the layers of the atmosphere from the ground upwards

questions.q: Climate is the average weather of a place over
questions.a: a long period, usually thirty years or more
o: a long period, usually thirty years or more
a single day, with its sunshine and its rain
one week, with its changes of heat and cold
one hour, with its changes of wind and cloud

questions.q: The movement of air from a high-pressure area to a low-pressure area is called ____.
questions.a: wind

questions.q: The five elements of weather and climate are
questions.a: temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind and atmospheric pressure
o: temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind and atmospheric pressure
rocks, rivers, lakes, hills and plains
sun, moon, stars, planets and comets
sand, soil, clay, gravel and silt

questions.q: Temperature decreases from the equator towards the poles because
questions.a: insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles
o: insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles
the poles are nearer the Sun than the equator is
the equator has no Sun during any part of the year
winds are stronger at the poles and cool the land

questions.q: Humidity is
questions.a: the presence of water vapour in the air
o: the presence of water vapour in the air
the temperature of the air at a given place
the speed at which the wind is blowing
the pressure that the air exerts on the ground

questions.q: Low-pressure areas are usually associated with
questions.a: cloudy skies and wet weather
o: clear sunny skies and dry weather over a wide region
no wind at all, with the air lying still
snow only, in every season of the year

questions.q: A high-pressure area forms where air is
questions.a: cold and heavy and sinks

questions.q: Distinguish between weather and climate.
questions.a: Weather is the hour-to-hour and day-to-day condition of the atmosphere, which changes quickly. Climate is the average of weather conditions over a large area for a long period, usually thirty years or more.
s: Climate defined with the long period

questions.q: Rain, drizzle, snow, sleet and hail are all forms of
questions.a: precipitation

questions.q: A wind blowing from the west is called a ____ wind.
questions.a: westerly

questions.q: A sea breeze blows
questions.a: from sea to land during the day
o: from sea to land during the day
from land to sea at night, when the land is cooler
from land to land across the plains during the day
only in deserts, where the sand heats up quickly

questions.q: Explain why a land breeze blows at night.
questions.a: At night land cools faster than the sea, so the air over the sea is warmer and has lower pressure, and the wind blows from land to sea.
s: Land cools faster than the sea at night
Wind blows from land to sea

questions.q: Explain why a sea breeze blows in the afternoon.
questions.a: During the day the land becomes warmer than the sea. A low-pressure region forms over land, so wind blows from the sea to the land.
s: Land warmer than sea causes low pressure over land
Wind blows from sea to land

questions.q: Explain how air pressure changes with height and how differences in pressure cause winds.
questions.a: Air pressure is highest at sea level and falls rapidly as altitude increases. In warm areas air rises and creates low pressure; in cold areas air sinks and creates high pressure. Air always moves from high to low pressure, and this movement is wind.
s: Warm areas low pressure and cold areas high pressure
Air moves from high to low pressure as wind

questions.q: When the air gets warmer, its capacity to hold water vapour
questions.a: increases, leading to higher humidity
o: decreases to zero, so the air becomes completely dry
does not change, whatever the temperature of the air
becomes negative, so the air takes water from the ground

questions.q: Why do we feel uncomfortable on a very humid day?
questions.a: The air already holds a lot of water vapour, so clothes take longer to dry and sweat evaporates more slowly.

questions.q: Explain how precipitation is formed and what affects it.
questions.a: When a part of the atmosphere is saturated with water vapour, the vapour condenses and falls under gravity as drizzle, rain, snow, sleet or hail. Prevailing winds, mountains and seasons are the main factors affecting precipitation.
s: Falls as rain, snow or hail under gravity

questions.q: Sam says the climate of a place is the weather on a particular day. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Weather is the condition on a particular day. Climate is the average over a long period, usually thirty years or more.
s: Distinguishes climate as a long-term average

questions.q: Plan a two-week weather log from a newspaper report. State what elements you would record and one pattern you may look for.
questions.a: Record daily temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind direction and speed and cloud cover. Look for patterns such as hotter days with low humidity or rain following low pressure.
s: Says to record daily for two weeks
Names a pattern to look for

concepts.name: The seasons of India
concepts.description: India's tropical monsoon climate, the four seasons recognised by the Indian Meteorological Department and the traditional six seasons.
concepts.idea: India has a tropical monsoon climate with four IMD seasons and, traditionally, six seasons of about two months each.
concepts.rule: IMD seasons: winter (December to early April), summer or pre-monsoon (April to June), monsoon (June to September), post-monsoon (October to December). Himalayan states have autumn and spring too. Traditional six seasons: Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta, Shishira.
concepts.example: The coldest months are December and January, with north-west India around 10-15 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: The climate of India can be broadly classified as
questions.a: tropical monsoon

questions.q: How many seasons does the Indian Meteorological Department recognise?
questions.a: four

questions.q: The monsoon season generally spans from June to ____.
questions.a: September

questions.q: Traditionally India experiences
questions.a: six seasons of about two months each
o: six seasons of about two months each
two seasons, a hot season and a cold season
four equal seasons of about three months each
twelve seasons, one for each month of the year

questions.q: The coldest months of the year in India are
questions.a: December and January

questions.q: The summer or pre-monsoon season lasts from
questions.a: April to June

questions.q: The post-monsoon season lasts from
questions.a: October to December

questions.q: The Himalayan states, being more temperate, have two additional seasons called
questions.a: autumn and spring

questions.q: List the four IMD seasons of India with their months.
questions.a: Winter: December to early April. Summer or pre-monsoon: April to June. Monsoon: June to September. Post-monsoon: October to December.

questions.q: In northern India the hottest month is generally
questions.a: May

questions.q: In the traditional calendar, Varsha (the rainy season) covers July to ____.
questions.a: August

questions.q: In western and southern India the hottest month is
questions.a: April

questions.q: Name the six traditional Indian seasons.
questions.a: Vasanta (spring), Grishma (summer), Varsha (monsoon), Sharad (early autumn), Hemanta (late autumn), Shishira (winter).

questions.q: What is the average temperature in inland India during summer, and how does winter differ in the north-west?
questions.a: In summer most of inland India averages 32-40 degrees Celsius. In winter the north-west averages around 10-15 degrees Celsius in the coldest months.

questions.q: Describe the monsoon (rainy) season and the post-monsoon season in India.
questions.a: The monsoon season is from June to September, dominated by the humid south-west summer monsoon. Rain recedes from north India from the beginning of October. The post-monsoon season lasts from October to December; in the north-west October and November are usually cloudless, and South India receives more rain then.

questions.q: What does the arrangement of the traditional Indian calendar into six seasons show?
questions.a: It is based on dividing the 12 months into six parts
o: It is based on dividing the 12 months into six parts
It ignores nature and follows only the dates of the calendar
It has only two parts, a wet part and a dry part
It is exactly the same as the seasons used by the IMD

questions.q: Why do the traditional seasons and the IMD seasons differ in number?
questions.a: The traditional seasons divide the 12 months astronomically into six parts of about two months each, while the IMD groups the year into four seasons based on overall weather patterns.
s: IMD seasons: four based on weather patterns

questions.q: Explain how the year is divided into seasons and why the climate is called tropical monsoon.
questions.a: Weather fluctuates within a day, so the year is divided by common patterns over weeks or months such as cool or hot, windy or calm, wet or dry. India's climate is tropical monsoon because it is strongly influenced by seasonal monsoon winds that bring most rain in one season.
s: Seasons based on common patterns over weeks or months
Links tropical monsoon to seasonal winds and rain

questions.q: Riya says India has only two seasons, hot and cold. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. The IMD recognises four seasons (winter, summer, monsoon, post-monsoon) and traditionally there are six seasons.
s: Gives four IMD or six traditional seasons

questions.q: Make a table for your region with the season, months and one feature of each of the four IMD seasons.
questions.a: Winter (Dec to early Apr): cool, coldest in Dec-Jan. Summer (Apr-Jun): hot and dry. Monsoon (Jun-Sep): humid with heavy rain. Post-monsoon (Oct-Dec): retreating monsoon, clear skies.

concepts.name: The monsoon
concepts.description: The meaning and mechanism of the south-west and north-east monsoons, their importance for Indian life and how monsoon knowledge and prediction developed.
concepts.idea: Monsoon winds reverse with the season because land and sea heat and cool at different rates.
concepts.rule: The word monsoon comes from the Arabic mausim (season). South-west monsoon (June to September): land heats faster, low pressure over India, moist winds from the ocean. Winter or north-east monsoon (October to February): land cools faster, cold dry winds from land to sea, but rain on the east coast after crossing the Bay of Bengal.
concepts.example: Most of India's agriculture depends on monsoon rain.

questions.q: The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word
questions.a: mausim

questions.q: The south-west monsoon blows between
questions.a: June and September

questions.q: The word mausim means ____.
questions.a: season

questions.q: The south-west monsoon is also known as the
questions.a: summer monsoon

questions.q: The south-west monsoon is mainly caused by
questions.a: unequal heating of land and the sea
o: unequal heating of land and the sea
earthquakes, which shake the land and the sea
ocean tides, which rise and fall every day
the Moon, whose pull raises the water of the sea

questions.q: During the south-west monsoon, the Indian subcontinent has
questions.a: low pressure

questions.q: The north-east monsoon blows from
questions.a: October to February

questions.q: The north-east monsoon brings rain mainly to
questions.a: Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka on the east coast
o: Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka on the east coast
the western desert, where the winter winds bring heavy rain
the Himalayan snow fields, which receive rain in winter
the north-west plains, which receive most of the winter rain

questions.q: Explain how the south-west monsoon is formed.
questions.a: In summer the Indian landmass heats faster than the oceans, creating low pressure over the land while the Indian Ocean stays cooler with high pressure. Moist winds blow from the ocean towards the land and bring rain.
s: Land heats faster, low pressure over India
Moist winds move from high to low pressure bringing rain

questions.q: Which monsoon accounts for most of India's rainfall?
questions.a: the south-west monsoon

questions.q: The north-east monsoon is also called the ____ monsoon.
questions.a: winter

questions.q: The winter monsoon winds usually do not bring rain to most parts of India because they are
questions.a: cold and dry, blowing from land to sea
o: cold and dry, blowing from land to sea
blowing from the sea, and carry a lot of moisture
very warm, and blowing from the south-west over the land
blowing from the south-west, and full of moisture

questions.q: How does the north-east monsoon bring rain to the east coast?
questions.a: The winds pass over the Bay of Bengal, pick up moisture and cause rain on the eastern coast, especially in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka.
s: Winds cross the Bay of Bengal and pick up moisture
Rain on the east coast, naming a state

questions.q: Give two ways monsoon affects people's lives.
questions.a: Agriculture depends on monsoon rain, and a good monsoon gives enough food and water in rivers, reservoirs and wells. It affects transport, festivals and employment, mainly in rural areas.
s: One effect such as agriculture or water supply
A second effect such as transport, festivals or jobs

questions.q: Explain how monsoon can be both a blessing and a problem.
questions.a: A good monsoon ensures food production and water supply for rivers, reservoirs and wells. Excessive rainfall can cause floods and weak monsoons can lead to droughts, so the economy, lifestyle and livelihoods depend on it.

questions.q: Ancient sailors noticed the monsoon because
questions.a: the reversal of winds helped their sailing ships
o: the reversal of winds helped their sailing ships
the sea froze in winter so that ships could not sail
the wind never changed, so ships kept the same course
rain stopped for many months so ships could not sail

questions.q: What methods did Indians use to predict rainfall in ancient times?
questions.a: Krishiparashara used the positions of the Moon and the Sun in the sky. Varahamihira in the Brihatsamhita used lunar mansions (nakshatras) to predict seasonal rainfall.

questions.q: Compare the south-west monsoon and the north-east monsoon.
questions.a: South-west (summer) monsoon: June to September, land heats faster than sea, moist winds blow from sea to land, brings most of India's rain. North-east (winter) monsoon: October to February, land cools faster, cold dry winds blow from land to sea and bring rain only to the south-eastern coast after crossing the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: Ali says the monsoon blows from land to sea all year. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Monsoon winds are seasonal: the summer monsoon blows from sea to land and the winter monsoon from land to sea.
s: Says monsoon winds reverse with the season

questions.q: Describe in your own words how monsoon affects the lives of people in your region, using three aspects.
questions.a: Farming depends on the rains for sowing and growing crops, water levels in wells and rivers rise, and festivals, travel and jobs are affected, especially in rural areas.

concepts.name: Climate change, carbon footprint and the Punjab floods
concepts.description: Climate change and greenhouse gases, actions to reduce the carbon footprint, and the natural and human-made causes and effects of the 2025 floods in Punjab.
concepts.idea: Human activities add greenhouse gases that trap heat and raise temperatures, and floods show how natural and human factors combine.
concepts.rule: Climate change is a long-term change in weather patterns caused mainly by human activities: burning fossil fuels, deforestation and industrial pollution. Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour. Reduce the carbon footprint by saving energy, using renewable energy, planting trees and living sustainably.
concepts.example: Punjab floods 2025: heavy monsoon rain and western disturbances (natural) and weak embankments, building near rivers, silt and late warnings (human-made).

questions.q: Climate change is
questions.a: a long-term change in weather patterns such as temperature, rainfall and wind
o: a long-term change in weather patterns such as temperature, rainfall and wind
a change in weather from hour to hour during the day
a change of season, from summer to the rainy season
a change in the Moon, from new moon to full moon

questions.q: Climate change is caused mainly by
questions.a: human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation
o: human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation
volcanoes only, which throw gases into the air
the Moon, whose pull changes the air of the Earth
ocean tides, which rise and fall every day

questions.q: Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide are ____ gases.
questions.a: greenhouse

questions.q: Which rivers of Punjab were flowing high before the 2025 floods?
questions.a: Satluj, Beas, Ravi and Ghaggar
o: Ganga and Yamuna, which flow through the northern plains
Godavari and Krishna, which flow through the peninsula
Narmada and Tapti, which flow to the Arabian Sea

questions.q: Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
questions.a: trap heat and raise global temperatures
o: trap heat and raise global temperatures
cool the Earth by reflecting heat back into space
remove clouds from the sky and dry the air
stop the wind and keep the air still

questions.q: Effects of climate change include
questions.a: more floods and droughts, melting glaciers and rising sea levels
o: more floods and droughts, melting glaciers and rising sea levels
shorter nights and longer days throughout the year

fewer stars visible in the sky at night

questions.q: Which action helps to reduce the carbon footprint?
questions.a: using renewable energy and planting trees
o: using renewable energy and planting trees
burning more fuel in vehicles and factories
cutting forests to make land for farms and towns
using single-use plastic for packing and carrying goods

questions.q: The natural causes of the 2025 Punjab floods included
questions.a: very heavy monsoon rains intensified by western disturbances
o: very heavy monsoon rains intensified by western disturbances
an earthquake in the hills, which caused the rivers to rise
a volcano in the Himalaya, which melted the snow
a cyclone from the east only, without any monsoon rain

questions.q: What are greenhouse gases and how do they raise temperatures?
questions.a: Gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour. They trap heat in the atmosphere and so raise global temperatures.
s: They trap heat and raise temperatures

questions.q: Burning of fossil fuels releases
questions.a: carbon dioxide

questions.q: In the carbon footprint activity, low impact choices score ____ point.
Which was a human-made cause of the Punjab floods?
questions.a: weak and old embankments (dhusi bandh)
o: western disturbances, which bring rain from the west
heavy monsoon rain over the hills and the plains
high river levels before the rain, from earlier rain

questions.q: Give two human-made causes of the 2025 Punjab floods.
questions.a: Weak and old embankments, houses and farms built too close to rivers, silt and mud reducing the capacity of rivers and dams, and late or unclear flood warnings.

questions.q: Give two effects of the Punjab floods.
questions.a: People lost their lives and thousands left their homes; farmland and paddy crops were damaged; poultry and dairy farms were destroyed; roads and bridges were damaged; standing water caused disease.

questions.q: Suggest three ways an individual can reduce his or her carbon footprint.
questions.a: Walk or cycle or use public transport, switch off electrical appliances when not in use, save water, and reuse, recycle and avoid single-use plastics.

questions.q: Poor flood warnings made the damage worse because
questions.a: people were unprepared

questions.q: Why did building houses and farms close to rivers worsen the Punjab floods?
questions.a: It reduced the natural space where floodwater could spread safely, so more homes and fields were in the water's path.

questions.q: Explain how both natural and human-made factors contributed to the Punjab floods of 2025.
questions.a: Natural: very heavy monsoon rain with western disturbances in Punjab, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir, and rivers already flowing high. Human-made: weak old embankments, building near rivers, silt reducing capacity and late warnings. Together they increased the damage.
s: Says they combined to increase damage

questions.q: Vik says climate change is only a natural process and people do not cause it. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. The chapter says climate change is caused mainly by human activities such as burning fossil fuels, deforestation and industrial pollution that raise greenhouse gases.

questions.q: Write a short Climate Action Pledge with two changes you will make to reduce your carbon footprint and why each helps.
